introduction-why-we-model-threats.core: Threat modeling is structured thinking about what can go wrong before you build. Adam Shostack's four questions frame it: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job? It catches design flaws (missing auth between services, trusting a header) that no scanner finds, and is cheapest during design. The output is a list of threats with mitigations, owners and tracked decisions.

first_principles.problem: A new microservice trusts an `X-User-Id` header from the gateway, but it's also reachable directly, so anyone can impersonate users.
truths: Design flaws are invisible to scanners.

analogy.title: A pre-flight checklist
analogy.story: Pilots don't wait for something to fail mid-air; they systematically ask what could go wrong before take-off.
analogy.breaks: Aircraft checklists are fixed; each system's threat model is unique.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The header-trust flaw is found before code is written.

code.text:
1. (10m) Draw the DFD on a whiteboard
2. (25m) Walk each trust boundary with STRIDE
3. (15m) Rank: likelihood x impact
4. (10m) File tickets with owners

Threat: service reachable bypassing gateway (Spoofing)
Mitigation: NetworkPolicy + verify signed JWT, not header

check.q: Why can't scanners replace threat modeling?
check.a: Scanners find implementation bugs; threat modeling finds flawed design assumptions and missing controls.

data-flow-diagrams-the-foundation-of-thr.core: A data flow diagram (DFD) shows how data moves through a system using four elements: external entities (users, third parties), processes (services), data stores (databases, queues) and data flows (arrows), plus trust boundaries where privilege or ownership changes. Threats cluster at trust boundaries, because that is where data crosses from less to more trusted zones. A DFD keeps the threat discussion concrete and reveals forgotten flows.

first_principles.problem: A team threat-models from memory and forgets the nightly export to a vendor's SFTP server.
truths: You can't protect what you haven't drawn.
derivation: Label flows with **protocol and data type**.
Store it **as code** to keep it current.

analogy.title: A plumbing schematic
analogy.story: Before finding leaks, you need a map of where water enters, which pipes it flows through, and where tanks and valves sit.
analogy.breaks: Pipes are fixed; software flows change with each release, so DFDs must be updated.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The vendor flow is visible and gets its own review.

check.q: Why focus threat analysis on trust boundaries?
check.a: That's where data moves between different privilege levels, so it's where checks are needed and often missing.

stride-a-framework-for-categorizing-thre.core: STRIDE is a mnemonic for six threat categories, each the violation of a security property: Spoofing (authenticity), Tampering (integrity), Repudiation (non-repudiation), Information disclosure (confidentiality), Denial of service (availability) and Elevation of privilege (authorization). Walking each DFD element and boundary through STRIDE turns 'what could go wrong?' into a systematic checklist, and each category maps to typical mitigations.

first_principles.problem: Brainstorming finds only the threats people already know about, leaving gaps like missing audit logs.

analogy.title: A doctor's systematic examination
analogy.story: Instead of guessing, they check heart, lungs, reflexes and so on, so nothing is missed.
analogy.breaks: Bodies are similar; systems differ, so some categories need creative thinking.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Six concrete threats from one arrow.

code.text:
| Cat | Threat                                  | Mitigation                |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| S   | Caller fakes X-User-Id header           | Verify signed JWT         |
| T   | Body altered in transit                 | mTLS                      |
| R   | User denies placing order               | Immutable audit log       |
| I   | Error leaks stack trace                 | Generic errors            |
| D   | Flood of large orders                   | Rate limit + size limits  |
| E   | Normal user calls /admin/refund         | Role check in service     |

check.q: Which STRIDE category does a missing audit log enable?
check.a: Repudiation: a user can deny an action because there's no reliable record.

visualizing-attacks-attack-trees.core: An attack tree puts an attacker's goal at the root (such as 'read customer PII') and decomposes it into sub-goals and concrete steps, using OR nodes (any child works) and AND nodes (all children are needed). Annotating leaves with cost, skill or likelihood shows the cheapest path, which is where defences matter most. Trees complement STRIDE by thinking from the attacker's objective rather than the system's components.

first_principles.problem: A team hardens the database heavily while the easiest route to the data is phishing an admin with no MFA.

analogy.title: Planning a heist movie
analogy.story: The crew lists every way into the vault (tunnel, inside man, stolen keycard) and picks the easiest one.
analogy.breaks: Movie heists have one crew; real systems face many attackers trying all paths.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Phishing is cheapest, so MFA for admins becomes the top fix.

code.text:
flowchart TD
  R[Read customer PII] --> A{OR}
  A --> B[SQLi in search: $$$]
  A --> C[Phish admin: $]

check.q: What does an AND node mean for defenders?
check.a: Blocking any one child blocks that whole branch.

prioritizing-threats-the-dread-model-and.core: Threat lists need ranking, because time is limited. DREAD scores Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users and Discoverability (1–10 each), though it is subjective and largely retired at Microsoft. Simpler risk matrices of likelihood × impact (low/medium/high) are more common, and CVSS standardises severity for known vulns. Whatever the method, the goal is a consistent, defensible order with each risk mitigated, accepted with an owner, transferred or avoided.

first_principles.problem: Forty threats are found and the team argues for days about which to fix first.

analogy.title: Hospital triage
analogy.story: Nurses don't treat in arrival order; they sort by severity and urgency so the worst cases go first.
analogy.breaks: Triage is quick and clinical; risk scoring involves judgement and debate.

check.q: Why has DREAD fallen out of favour?
check.a: Its scores are subjective and inconsistent between assessors, giving false precision.

the-human-element-red-teaming-and-blue-t.core: Threat models are hypotheses; red and blue teams test them. A red team emulates real adversaries end to end (phishing, lateral movement, exfiltration) to test whether defences and people detect and respond. The blue team defends: detection engineering, monitoring and incident response. Purple teaming puts them together, replaying techniques (mapped to MITRE ATT&CK) and tuning detections in real time. The value is discovering what the paper model missed and measuring detection.

first_principles.problem: A threat model says lateral movement is 'mitigated', but a red team moves from a laptop to production in two days undetected.
truths: Detection must be tested, not assumed.
derivation: Feed findings back into the **threat model**.

analogy.title: A fire drill with a hidden 'fire'
analogy.story: You find out whether alarms work and people know the exits only by actually running the drill.
analogy.breaks: Drills are announced; good red-team exercises are often unannounced to staff.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Detection gaps are found and closed with evidence.

code.text:
# emulate T1003.001 (LSASS credential dumping)
Invoke-AtomicTest T1003.001 -TestNumbers 1
# blue team checks: did the EDR/SIEM rule fire? how fast?
# if not, write or fix the detection and re-run

check.a: Red and blue teams working together to run attacks and immediately validate or improve detections.
